judgments.reasoning_cat1: The installment refund variant states payments continue until the sum equals the proceeds applied and then for life; the arithmetic is self-executing. No term with competing meanings appears.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It fits within Option 3 (c040) and is consistent with the option tables and the commutation rule at c046.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Option 4 survives only as a rule that the final payment equals the unpaid balance plus a right to withdraw; both are definite mechanics. Nothing nameable is ambiguous.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It matches the c046 rule that for options 1 and 4 the amount then due is any balance held by the insurer.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Option 5's text is heavily degraded but its substance, income for two payees by reference to the page 5 table, is straightforward. The table reference supplies the amounts.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The page 5 tables are headed for a 'male' age and the availability note at c012 says the option is available for two males or two females, a small mismatch, but the note resolves it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The Joint and 2/3 variant is legible enough in substance: full payment while both live, reduced payment thereafter, though the fraction itself is lost in the OCR. The concept is a standard survivor reduction.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is consistent with Option 5 (c043) and the option 5 table, and nothing elsewhere states a different survivor fraction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Rates at least as liberal as those we charge as of the option date for a single premium immediate annuity of the same kind' turns on the vague comparators 'as liberal as' and 'of the same kind'. Those are nameable soft standards left to the insurer's own rate book.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It overrides the page 5 tables and interacts with the commutation-rate sentence in c046, which expressly contemplates a specified rate for alternate life income, so the two are coordinated.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The provision is specific: a single payment to the last payee's estate, balance for options 1 and 4, commuted present value at 4.5% for options 2, 3 and 5. The only softness is the promise to 'specify' a commutation rate for alternate income.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The 4.5% commutation rate sits against the 3% actuarial basis stated at c013 and the option 1 interest floor at c038, which a payee could argue produces an inconsistent measure of value, though the two rates serve different functions.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The conversion promise survives only as a truncated right to convert without proving insurability, so the conditions on the right cannot be read. The no-evidence promise itself is definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It stands against 'Proof You Can Be Insured' (c020), which requires proof acceptable to the insurer, and the two are reconciled only by treating conversion as an exception that the text does not spell out.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The conversion date sentence is cut through the middle so the outer limit on 'any time' and the effective date rule are unreadable. What survives is a mechanical 'later of' rule.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It interlocks with the Notice provision at c052 (request within 31 days before the conversion date) and with the final term date in Renewal (c024), and no conflict is visible.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The new contract may be any whole life plan 'that we' (offer, presumably), an insurer-controlled menu whose scope is not stated. The truncation leaves the qualifier unknown.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It works with the Amount and Premium provisions (c050, c051), which likewise refer to the insurer's then-published rates and minimum issue limits.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The amount rule is bounded at both ends, no more than the converted part and no less than the minimum whole life issue limit, and both bounds are objective. 'The converted part of this contract' is a mildly soft phrase but is workable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It coordinates with the If Disabled provision (c054), which addresses what happens when the amount falls below the minimum issue limit, so the two are complementary.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Premium at 'our then published rates for such plan and your age at that time' is a definite external referent, and the risk-class carry-over sentence is garbled but conventional. Nothing genuinely two-sided is nameable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The carry-over of the risk class fits the risk-class footnotes (c007, c008, c014) and the risk class definition stub (c021).

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The requirement to ask within 31 days before the conversion date and that the insured be alive both at conversion and at request is precise. The only oddity is the double aliveness condition, which is intelligible.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is consistent with the Notice definition (c016) requiring written form acceptable to the insurer and with the conversion date rule (c048).

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The riders paragraph piles up several negative conditions about waiver of premium, accidental death, issue-age limits and 'other riders if we agree', with a parenthetical exception for converting on the last allowed day. The stacked negatives and the residual 'other riders' discretion leave the reach of the restrictions uncertain.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It must be read with the If Disabled provision (c054) and with the Accelerated Benefit Rider, which the specification page shows attached at no charge, and whether that rider carries over to the new contract is not addressed.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The disability conversion rule is badly fragmented, mixing the last day allowed to convert, waived premiums, a plan chosen by the insurer and the minimum issue limit. What the insured must do and what the insurer does automatically cannot be separated on the words.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is an exception to the Amount rule (c050) and to the rider restrictions (c053), and it depends on a waiver of premium rider whose terms are not reproduced anywhere in this instrument.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Only the heading and the word 'contract' survive, so the carry-over rule for incontestability and suicide on conversion is entirely unreadable here. Whether periods run afresh on the new contract is exactly the point such a clause decides.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is the bridge between the Suicide (c034) and Incontestability (c033) periods and any successor contract, and in a replacement-policy dispute that bridge is where the contest over when the two-year clocks started would sit.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The rider's opening states that accelerated benefits reduce death proceeds and that premium reduces to the level 'appropriate for' the reduced proceeds, a soft but self-referencing standard. It cross-refers to Contract Values for the mechanics.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It duplicates the premium-reduction sentence at c072 and depends on the Contract Values formula (c070), which is itself incompletely reproduced, but the statements agree with each other.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'If the rider and contract differ, the rider controls' is a short priority rule whose scope, whether it covers all differences or only rider subject matter, is not spelled out. It is exactly the kind of one-line supremacy clause parties argue about.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It governs real overlaps such as the competing definitions of 'you' at c019 and c059 and the proceeds payment options at c069 versus c035, so its reach across the whole instrument matters.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The effective date is the later of the contract effective date and something now lost to the OCR, so the second limb cannot be identified. The 'later of' construction is otherwise mechanical.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It ties to the contract date on the specification page and to Contract Months and Years (c015), and no other provision states a different rider start.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The rider's pronoun definition makes 'you' the insured but the owner for contract rights, a deliberate double meaning stated in fragments. The split is signposted rather than hidden.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It restates and slightly varies the policy's Pronouns provision (c019), with the rider-controls clause (c057) resolving any difference, so the fit is provided for.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The physician definition is bounded by licensure and by an enumerated list of excluded relatives plus 'a member of your household'. The relative list is closed and the household limb is a familiar, workable standard.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It supports the Qualifying Requirements (c062) and the Medical Referee provision (c067), which uses the same concept consistently.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The benefits sentence is cut off before it states the amount payable, leaving only a reference to payment to the owner and to having more than one contract with the insurer. The aggregate limit across contracts cannot be read.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It depends on the Contract Values formula (c070) and the minimum issue limit condition in c062, both of which are themselves incomplete, so the benefit ceiling is not resolved anywhere in the instrument.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The qualifying conditions are presented as a list that 'all must apply', but the OCR has scrambled the items so that consents of other persons having rights, diagnosis, and in-force status run together. A conjunctive list of conditions is nonetheless a definite structure.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It builds on the Terminal Condition (c063) and Physician (c060) definitions and on the minimum issue limit also referenced at c050, and those references are consistent.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Terminal condition' is defined by 'non-correctable' and a life expectancy limb resting on 'reasonable medical certainty', with the period itself lost to the OCR. Medical-certainty prognosis language is a classic locus of genuine dispute.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It feeds the Qualifying Requirements (c062) and the Medical Referee mechanism (c067), which exists precisely because the diagnosis may be disputed, so the instrument anticipates rather than contradicts it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The definition of a request for payment is reduced to a stub referring to a written request and a terminal condition. Nothing contestable can be named in what survives.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It works with the Notice provision (c016) and with the additional-proof clause (c065) without inconsistency.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The insurer may require additional proof and an examination by its own physician at its expense; the discretion is broad but the cost allocation is definite. 'Additional proof' is open-ended in what it may demand.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It leads into the Medical Referee provision (c067) and the cost-sharing sentence at c068, which allocate the same expenses in overlapping terms.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A stub recommending consultation with a tax advisor before adding the rider or requesting payment; it is advisory rather than operative. There is nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It creates no obligation that could clash with any other provision of the policy or rider.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The referee mechanism is procedurally specific: a disinterested third physician acceptable to both, whose decision the insurer will accept, with a cost consequence if the decision favours the insured. 'Acceptable to both' could deadlock but the process is otherwise definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It presupposes the physician definition (c060) and the insurer's examination right (c065), and the cost sentence at c068 continues it; whether the referee's decision binds the insured as well as the insurer is left open across the two.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The cost-allocation sentence is fragmentary but says the insurer pays for its own physician and, if the decision favours the insured, for the insured's physician's time. The condition is stated in the preceding paragraph rather than here.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is a continuation of the Medical Referee provision (c067) and overlaps with the 'at our expense' language in c065, with no contradiction between them.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Payment is in a lump sum or, at the owner's choice, under 'any proceeds payment option contained in the contract except those which are contingent on the life of the insured'. The exception is a general carve-out against the enumerated options, and which of options 1 to 5 it excludes has to be worked out rather than read.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Applying it requires going to options 1 through 5 (c038-c044) and asking which are life-contingent, and the rule at c035 that a death-proceeds payee must be the beneficiary does not fit an accelerated payment to the owner.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The Contract Values formula survives only as disconnected pieces ('A is the benefit paid under this rider', '$100', 'state where this rider is issued'), so the reduction cannot be computed from the text. A formula whose terms are missing is unusable on its face.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is the mechanism invoked by c056 and c072 for reducing death proceeds and premiums, so its incompleteness undermines those cross-references, and the interest rate provision (c071) supplies only one input.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The rate cap is tied to an identified external index with a named fallback if that index is not published, which is a carefully bounded formula. The fallback, 'a substantially similar average acceptable to the state insurance commissioner', is soft but conditioned on an outside approval.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It supplies an input to the Contract Values calculation (c070) and does not conflict with the 3% actuarial basis (c013) or the option 1 interest rate (c038), which govern different payments.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The sentence says premiums reduce to the level required for the reduced death proceeds, a definite consequence, marred only by a duplicated 'will will'. The doubling is a transcription slip that does not change meaning.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It restates the premium-reduction promise already made at c056 and depends on the Contract Values reduction (c070); the repetition is consistent rather than conflicting.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The termination list is introduced as 'earliest of' but only two of its items survive, so the full set of triggers cannot be checked. An 'earliest of' construction is otherwise mechanical.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It depends on when 'the contract terminates', which the Grace Period clause (c023) fixes retroactively at the premium due date, so a lapse could be read as having ended the rider before a pending accelerated benefit request.
